summary: Rock Island's stone light at the Green Bay entrance, begun in the 1830s and rebuilt in 1858; volunteers now run its keepers' house as a museum after the light went dark.

structures.note: Two-story coursed rubble building with an attached frame addition; the nomination describes the building as the 1858 rebuilding (it gives 1839 per Coast Guard drawings, see resolved conflicts).
1858 tower on the dwelling's northern gable; LighthouseFriends describes a square wooden tower with a nine-sided lantern and the nomination a stone building with a square tower base.
Steel skeleton tower near the lighthouse, installed by the Coast Guard to display the light (LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Reached by passenger ferry from Washington Island and a 1.2-mile hike; tours daily 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. from Memorial Day weekend to Columbus Day (LighthouseFriends).

visit.note: Dwelling and tower open in season, with docent-led tours.

stay.provider: Friends of Rock Island State Park
stay.note: Volunteer docents live in the lighthouse for week-long stints in season (LighthouseFriends, from 2004). The FORI docent page recruits volunteers and sets a 31 December application deadline; confirm the rules with the operator.

facts.agency: Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources (owner, per LighthouseFriends); Friends of Rock Island State Park (museum operator)

events.note: Congress appropriates $5,000 for the lighthouse; a further $3,000 the next year.
Contract signed 2 April 1836 for a conical stone or brick tower with a dwelling; 1836 is the station record's date.
Light completed and in service by 1837; David E. Corbin appointed first keeper 19 December 1837.
Original building constructed in 1839 according to Coast Guard drawings (nomination; conflicts with 1837).
Rebuilt after the earlier light washed away (1866 list, nomination); new dwelling and tower.
Converted from lard oil to kerosene.
Boathouse, boat ways and landing crib built.
Telephone cable laid to the station.
Brick oil house built.
Well drilled near the lighthouse.
June 16: keeper Edward H. Cornell and assistant John Fitzgerald aid two men in a disabled motor boat.
Illuminant changed from oil to incandescent oil vapour.
Last head keeper leaves; wet-cell batteries power the light and the dwelling is closed (LighthouseFriends; the USLHS gives 1966).
Automated (USLHS).
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, 20 April 1979.
Discontinued, per USLHS (1980s).
Solar panels replace the batteries.
Coast Guard installs a steel skeleton tower near the lighthouse to display the light.
New lantern room installed on the dwelling to replace the one removed by the Coast Guard.
Dedicated 17 May as the Pottawatomie Lighthouse Museum; volunteer docents live in the house.
Replica fourth-order Fresnel lens installed in the lantern room.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Construction date: the record gives 1836; LighthouseFriends says the light was completed by 1837 (a year after the territory was created) and USLHS gives 1837; the 1937 Bulletin says 'erected in 1837'; the nomination says the original building was constructed in 1839 per Coast Guard drawings and rebuilt in 1858. Not resolved; the story gives the contract (1836), the 1837 service and the nomination's 1839 claim.
Tower material of the 1858 light: the nomination and USLHS say stone or limestone; LighthouseFriends says a square wooden tower on the dwelling's northern gable. Not resolved.
Automation: LighthouseFriends dates the end of the resident keepers and the battery power to 1947; USLHS gives automation in 1966; the record gives 'automated as of 1966'. The story gives both.

Light status: the nomination (1977-79) says the light is still in use but automated; USLHS says discontinued in the 1980s with a battery beacon; LighthouseFriends says a steel tower displayed the light from 1988. The record gives inactive, deactivated 1989 (Rowlett). Not resolved.

notes_for_editor: (1) Dates: see resolved_conflicts (built 1836/1837/1839; automation 1947/1966; light status 1980/1988/1989). The record's focal height (48.5 m) and characteristic (Fl W 4s) are not confirmed by a source read here; LighthouseFriends gives the 1858 focal plane as 159 ft, USLHS gives 137 ft for the light above mean high water and the nomination 137 ft above sea level; not reconciled. (2) The 1876 logbook entries are quoted by LighthouseFriends; the logbook itself was not read. (3) Roster: USLHS lines copied as printed (32); LighthouseFriends adds Frederick W. Raether (1899). The relations of Emily Betts to William Betts come from LighthouseFriends ('married'); the relations of Paulina A. Capers and Mollie M. Boshka to the men they served under are not stated in any source, so none is claimed. (4) Living people: no roster name is after 1947; none is named beyond the roster. (5) Ownership: the nomination (1977) names the U.S. Coast Guard as owner; LighthouseFriends names the Wisconsin DNR (current); the transfer date is not sourced. (6) The record's 'stay: keeper_program' is supported by FORI's docent programme page; the 2027 season terms should be checked with FORI. (7) The 1894 Board volume is cited by scan page (printed page not confirmed). (8) Bulletin 1937 passage is in an article on the Ninth District with interleaved OCR columns; only the clean phrase is quoted. (9) Access: the nomination says the light is 'still in use'; the Lighthouse Society's record says the aid is not active; the story says the light is not an active aid, per LighthouseFriends' 'battery-powered beacon' and the 1980s discontinuance, and does not claim a current status. (7) Fact-check pass 2026-10-22: the FORI docent page recruits volunteers and does not say they live in the house; the live-in stints come from LighthouseFriends (2004). The 1876 wreck outcome no longer says bodies or May 1876: the LighthouseFriends text says the two men were seen several times and were still adrift at the last account, and the keeper's entry date is not given. The story's '1.2-mile hike' and '20 miles' are kept as printed; the NRHP and LighthouseFriends do not say whether the twenty miles is statute or nautical.
